strengths: Addresses an important problem: retaining information beyond a transformer's context window in offline reinforcement learning under partial observability.

The T-Maze ablation provides concrete evidence for MRV: at test length 900, success improves from 0.61 ± 0.07 without MRV to 0.90 ± 0.07 with MRV (Table 6). ViZDoom also shows substantial gains over DT.
The evaluation spans visual and vector observations, several memory tasks, Atari, and MuJoCo, with repeated training runs and reported uncertainty.

Includes useful ablations of memory corruption, cache size, memory-token count, alternative update mechanisms, and curriculum learning. Dataset descriptions, hyperparameters, and a code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Important comparisons are confounded. Appendix D removes the feed-forward block only for RATE and introduces segment-wise target-return resets for MuJoCo, while comparison scores use previously published protocols. These changes need independent ablations and equivalent baseline treatment before gains can be attributed to the proposed memory architecture.

The recurrent baselines are insufficiently validated. DLSTM, DGRU, and DMamba all achieve exactly chance performance on T-Maze at the training horizon of 90 steps. Without model-specific tuning details and convergence diagnostics, these failures do not justify broad conclusions about these architectures' memory limitations.

The claim of significant superiority across memory environments exceeds the evidence. Memory Maze improves only from RMT's 7.27 ± 0.21 to 7.64 ± 0.41, a small difference relative to the reported uncertainty. In Minigrid, TrXL performs better on smaller grids and RMT on larger grids. MuJoCo's aggregate score also remains below the strongest reported comparator.

The architectural novelty is limited: RATE combines established Decision Transformer, recurrent memory-token, and Transformer-XL mechanisms, while MRV uses standard cross-attention. Stronger positioning against existing memory-update methods and broader evidence for MRV's distinctive benefit are needed; the clearest retention results concern simple one-bit cues.

The claimed inequality R[OracleDT] ≥ R[RATE] ≥ R[DT] is not generally valid. A trained model receiving privileged information does not automatically upper-bound another trained architecture, and adding memory does not guarantee improvement over DT. Likewise, noise-injection experiments establish sensitivity to memory corruption but do not identify precisely what information is stored.

Technical reporting contains consequential gaps and inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 leaves cache updates and gradient propagation between segments unspecified. Appendix G's parameter-overhead formula counts only memory embeddings, omitting MRV projection weights and failing to account for RATE's feed-forward-block removal. This weakens reproducibility and the interpretation of efficiency comparisons.
